newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN envoy cautions on U.S. stance on Iraq oil deal.
newsitem.headline: UN envoy cautions on U.S. stance on Iraq oil deal.

text.p: A senior U.N. official, who had said a rollover of the Iraq oil-for-food deal was a foregone conclusion, however cautioned later that the United States had not made up its mind yet.

"The United States and several others have said they had not made up their minds. Some others, like Russia, said there should be," Undersecretary-General Yasushi Akashi told reporters after briefing the Security Council.
The $2 billion six-month deal expires on June 7 and needs another Security Council resolution to extend it.

Akashi, in charge of the U.N. Department of Humanitarian Affairs, tempered his comments after speaking to council members. Before he went to a closed council session he told reporters he believed that a rollover of the oil-for-food deal was a "foregone conclusion," presumably on the same terms.
He said the Council still had to decide on the issue and it was "not our intention" to give a recommendation at this time, which would come from U.N. Undersecretary-General Kofi Annan.
Akashi will brief journalists Thursday on his recent trip to Iraq to observe implementation of the plan

A senior U.N. official told Reuters on Wednesday that U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan was expected to recommend by the end of the month that the deal be renewed in June on the same terms as the current six-month plan.

He said the United States had suggested some changes in dealing with Kurdish areas in the north, which have a separate allotment of food and medicine. But diplomats said no formal or informal proposal had been made by Washington.

The accord allows Iraq to sell up to $2 billion of oil over six months in order to purchase food, medicine and other goods for its people suffering under U.N. sanctions imposed when Baghdad's troops invaded Kuwait in August 1990.
About two-thirds of the monies are for the humanitarian supplies, with the remainder earmarked for compensation of Gulf War victims and the costs of destroying Iraq's weapons of mass destruction.
